text: Elder and Youth Perspectives of Country Foods in the Inuvialuit Settlement Region Maria Ramirez Prieto1, Sonja Ostertag1, Kelly Skinner1, Melissa Rogers2, Shayla Arey2, Kanelsa Noksana2, Alex Sayers2, Denise Wolki2, Kristin Green2, Susie Memogana2, Shelby Lucas2 1School of Public Health Sciences, University of Waterloo, 2Community Research Lead • Limited information on the past and current foods eaten • Youth are facing barriers to participating in subsistence harvesting [1-2], and a growing body of literature is documenting a dietary change away from country foods (CF) among younger generations

• Although CF consumption has been documented, it has been almost exclusively through quantitative methods, and qualitative studies have yet to have an exclusive lens exploring CF consumption in youth. experiences with CF consumption is essential for ensuring Inuit Knowledge and culture is maintained, and CF and Inuit Knowledge programs and strategies can be informed adequately.

We explored Elder and youth experiences in all six communities of the Inuvialuit Settlement Region (ISR) to Photovoice: Youth participants became co-researchers by taking photos of their experiences, ultimately co-leading Elders were interviewed on their past and current diets, Project Objectives 1) To explore how the Inuvialuit diet has changed.
To identify, age and culturally specific food security supports and barriers for Inuvialuit youth.
To amplify youth’s voices through participatory methods and dissemination products.

Approach: Community Based Participatory Action Research Study 1: Inuvialuit Elders Experiences within the CF system • Who: Elders (~55 years or older) (n = 46) • Data Collection: Storytelling and semi-structured interviews • Data Analysis: Reflexive Thematic Analysis Study 2: Inuvialuit Youth Experiences within the CF system • Who: Youth (13-30 years old) (n=9) • Data Collection: Photovoice • Date Analysis: Reflexive Thematic Analysis • Elders were primarily raised on the land and ate country food with an emphasis on eating and using the whole animal (meat, organs, hides, etc.) Today’s experiences with food • CF is preferred over store-bought foods • Many traditions are carried on today, including eating caribou head, and swan Many Elders depend on family or community members sharing to access CF 3. Cultural and traditional lifestyle changes • Change in harvesting and preparation practices • Staying out on the land for long periods of time is less common • Using the whole animal is less common • Climate change is making it difficult to harvest and access camps • Perceived generation difference of preferred foods • Change in sharing and gathering 4. Supporting youth through a cultural and traditional lifestyle • Learning on the land provides the best opportunity for youth to learn • High use of technology by youth is a concern • Not all youth have access to equipment 5. Importance of family for food security activities • Family, food programs, and sharing 2. Strong cultural skills and knowledge • All youth participant had strong knowledge about CF being healthy • Youth that harvested had strong cultural skills of noticing the land, water, air, and behaviour of animals • “Keep Learning, Keep Trying” –Kaydra Nogosak Youth expressed a desire for learning and passing on skills/knowledge 4. Concern about climate change • Youth are experiencing difficulties harvesting and accessing their camps due to climate change 5. Importance of family for food security 1. Halseth, R. (2015).
